dashboard.title: NBK Base-Rate Decision Forecast
dashboard.intro: How hard are six macro factors pushing the National Bank of Kazakhstan towards a rate hike or a cut? Read-only view of a fitted ordered-logit model; nothing is re-estimated here.
dashboard.unit: probability difference P(Increase) - P(Decrease), from −1 (cut certain) to +1 (hike certain)

dashboard.rounds_caption: Both rounds use the latest available factor values; future values are unknown, so the probabilities are identical and only the date differs.
dashboard.card_foot: Latest factor data as of 2026-10-27. Conditional model estimates; calibration is unverified.
why: **Same inputs for both rounds.** Both rounds use the latest available factor values (factor data month 2026-08), because future factor values are unknown. Both blocks are therefore the same conditional estimate: the probabilities are identical and only the date differs. This is not an error and not a separate forecast for each date.
**Why Hold is most likely.** Hold was the most common NBK decision in the sample: 49 of 91 decisions in data/processed/nbk_decisions_clean.csv.

**Hike or cut?** The 95% intervals (Increase 0.0%–18.9%, Decrease 4.2%–73.2%) are wide and overlap, and the score band -0.747 to +0.136 includes zero, so the model does not separate a hike from a cut at this date.

**Holdout comparison.** On the 18 holdout decisions the RMSE ratio is 0.995, below 1, so the model meets the pre-specified criterion against Always Hold. This does not show that the model forecasts better. The factors have a detectable link with the decisions (joint likelihood-ratio test p = 0.026). The margin is small; see the Evidence tab for its uncertainty.
dashboard.verdict_box: Ordered logit meets the pre-specified criterion against Always Hold on the holdout (RMSE ratio 0.995, below 1). This does not show that the model forecasts better. The 95% block-bootstrap interval for the RMSE ratio (0.780 to 1.335) contains 1, and the Diebold–Mariano test (HLN-corrected) gives p = 0.961, so on 18 holdout decisions the model cannot be distinguished from Always Hold in either direction. Effect of the data update (OLD = git tag before-data-update-2026-09-07, NEW = current files): usable decisions 88 → 89; estimation sample 70 → 71 decisions (ending 2024-06-03 → 2024-07-15); holdout 18 → 18 decisions (2024-07-15–2026-09-07 → 2024-09-02–2026-10-27). The holdout RMSE ratio changed from 1.002 to 0.995, so the pre-specified rule's label changed from "does not meet the pre-specified criterion (RMSE ratio not below 1)" to "meets the pre-specified criterion (RMSE ratio below 1)". 95% bootstrap intervals: OLD 0.828 to 1.230, NEW 0.780 to 1.335; both ratios lie inside both intervals, so the change does not show that the model forecasts better or worse than before.

decision_rule.head: Decision rule (option 1: direction flag (band clear of zero)), a monitoring rule, not a forecast.
decision_rule.text: Named user: a bank treasury analyst who, before an NBK base-rate meeting, needs to know whether the model shows a distinguishable tilt in rate pressure. if the 95% band of the score moves entirely above 0 (or entirely below 0), then flag a hawkish (or dovish) tilt and review rate-sensitive exposures before the next decision, because only then is the sign of the pressure distinguishable from balance, given a band about 0.883 score points wide. Today: the band is -0.747 to +0.136; triggered: no.

sentences: Headline RMSE ratio 0.995. The 95% block-bootstrap interval for the RMSE ratio (0.780 to 1.335) contains 1, and the Diebold–Mariano test (HLN-corrected) gives p = 0.961, so on 18 holdout decisions the model cannot be distinguished from Always Hold in either direction.

Supplementary measure (exploratory, added after the holdout had been seen; the pre-specified verdict stays RMSE-based): the ranked probability score on the same holdout (lower is better) is 0.154 for the model, 0.194 for Always Hold and 0.159 for the class frequencies of the estimation sample. Simple class frequencies do almost as well as the model, so the six factors add little beyond the base rates of cuts, holds and hikes; most of the gain over Always Hold comes from admitting that cuts and hikes happen.
Inside the estimation sample (rolling origin, no holdout data) the lowest RPS belongs to P0 — Policy-rule ordered logit: inflation, its 3-month change, real rate, previous decision (0.165).
Specifications with positive RPS skill in every design: M0, M1. Those whose skill turns negative in some design are not robust, whatever their best score.

Policy-inertia specifications (exploratory only; P0 = inflation, its 3-month change, the ex-post real rate and the previous decision; P1 = P0 plus the other five factors, ridge). P0 has the lower RPS in 1 of 3 designs; P1 has the lower RPS in 2 of 3 designs. The ranking depends on the evaluation design, which is instability, not an improvement; neither specification replaces the pre-specified model.
